subtitle: Remove interference before sampling: RC, active and Sallen-Key low-passes
takeaways: f_{c} = 1/(2πRC): −3 dB, −20 dB per decade per order
Op-amp buffers the filter: no loading, optional gain
Anti-aliasing low-pass with f_{c} ≤ f_{s}/2 before the S&H

slides.title: RC low-pass and high-pass
bullets: Low-pass: frequency-dependent divider, C shorts high frequencies
At f_{c}: |H| = 0.707 (−3 dB), phase −45° (high-pass: +45°)
Above f_{c}: −20 dB per decade (10× frequency → 1/10 amplitude)
High-pass blocks DC: coupling capacitor, +20 dB/decade below f_{c}
dB = 20·log_{10}|H|: cascaded gains add in dB
slides.notes: Show the Bode plot: two straight asymptotes meeting at f_{c}. Derivation of H(jω), the dB table and the high-pass formula are in section Passive RC Filters. Remind them that τ = RC and f_{c} are two views of the same thing.

slides.title: Falstad: RC low-pass and high-pass

falstad.name: filter_rc_lowpass
falstad.hint: Compare amplitudes at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 10 kHz (f_{c} = 995 Hz)

falstad.name: filter_rc_highpass
falstad.hint: Same R, C swapped: watch the phase lead of +45° at 1 kHz

observe: Low-pass: 0.995 V, 0.705 V, 0.099 V at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 10 kHz
High-pass mirrors it: 0.100 V, 0.709 V, 0.995 V
Add a load resistor at the output: f_{c} and amplitude shift
slides.notes: R = 1.6 kΩ, C = 100 nF. Point out the limits of passive filters: the load changes f_{c}, no gain. This motivates the op-amp in the next section. Exercise 7.1 works the numbers.

slides.title: First-order active filters
bullets: Non-inverting: RC low-pass, then follower or amplifier G = 1 + R_{2}/R_{1}
Op-amp input does not load C; output drives the next stage
Inverting low-pass: C parallel to R_{2}, f_{c} = 1/(2πR_{2}C), gain −R_{2}/R_{1}
Inverting high-pass: C_{1} in series with R_{1}, f_{c} = 1/(2πR_{1}C_{1})
slides.rule: f_{c} is set by the R and C that form the filter

falstad.name: filter_active_first_order
falstad.hint: Three filters, 0.1 V at 1 kHz: compare Vout_a, Vout_b, Vout_c

slides.notes: Falstad values: non-inverting LP with G = 2 gives 0.141 V, inverting LP and HP with gain −10 give about 0.705 V. Circuits of the inverting variants are on the next script pages; Exercise 7.2.

slides.title: The integrator
bullets: C in the feedback path: V_{out} = −(1/RC)·∫V_{in} dt
−20 dB per decade at all frequencies, DC gain infinite
Any offset drives a pure integrator into saturation
Practical: R_{p} parallel to C limits DC gain to −R_{p}/R
slides.rule: Square wave in → triangle out, slope V_{in}/(RC)

falstad.name: filter_integrator
falstad.hint: ±1 V square at 500 Hz: triangle of 1 V p-p; watch R_{p} centre it

slides.notes: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 nF: slope 1000 V/s, 1 V per ms. The triangle starts between 0 and −1 V and is centred slowly by R_{p} (τ = 0.1 s). Exercise 7.3.

slides.title: Sallen-Key low-pass (unity gain)
bullets: Order n: −20·n dB per decade; 2nd order with one op-amp
C_{1} to the output gives positive feedback near f_{0}
Q sets the corner: 0.707 Butterworth = maximally flat, −3 dB at f_{0}
Higher Q: peaking and ringing; |H(f_{0})| = Q
slides.notes: At 20·f_{c} a first-order filter gives −26 dB, second order −52 dB. Transfer function and comparison of coefficients are in section Second-Order Filters. Higher orders: cascade of second-order stages with tabulated f_{0} and Q.

slides.title: Design recipe: Butterworth Sallen-Key
steps: Choose R_{1} = R_{2} = R; Q = 0.707 needs C_{1} = 2·C_{2} (C_{1} to the output)
Pick C_{2} from E6, C_{1} ≈ 2·C_{2} (e.g. 10 nF and 22 nF: Q = 0.74)
Calculate R = 1/(2πf_{0}√(C_{1}C_{2})), round to E24 or E96
Check f_{0} and Q with rounded values; use film or C0G capacitors
slides.notes: Capacitors come in coarser steps, so choose them first. Q between 0.65 and 0.75 changes the response by less than 1 dB. Example 1 kHz: 10 nF, 22 nF, 10.7 kΩ gives f_{0} = 1003 Hz, Q = 0.742.

slides.title: Falstad: first vs. second order

falstad.name: filter_sallen_key
falstad.hint: At 10 kHz: RC passes 99 mV, Sallen-Key only 10 mV

observe: Near the corner (1 kHz) both are similar: 0.705 V vs. 0.744 V
One decade above: −20 dB vs. −40 dB
Change C_{1} to raise Q and watch the peaking
slides.notes: Input 1 V amplitude; RC with f_{c} = 995 Hz, Sallen-Key with f_{0} = 1003 Hz, Q = 0.742. Exercise 7.4.

slides.section: The Anti-Aliasing Filter of the Capstone
slides.title: Why filter before sampling?
bullets: Only frequencies below f_{s}/2 are reproduced correctly
Capstone: f_{s} = 5 Hz → f_{c} ≤ 2.5 Hz (2.34 Hz chosen)
Above f_{s}/2 a component reappears at a wrong low frequency (aliasing)
50 Hz hum: 4.9 mV at the bridge × 107.6 = 0.52 V at the INA output
After sampling nothing separates alias from signal: filter first
slides.rule: f_{c} ≤ f_{s}/2, filter before the S&H
slides.notes: Preview of the ADC chapter. 50 Hz = 10·f_{s}: the samples see the hum at a fixed phase; if mains drifts to 50.1 Hz the error becomes a slow 0.1 Hz wave in the data.

slides.section: The Anti-Aliasing Filter of the Capstone
slides.title: Capstone filter: 1st vs. 2nd order

left.head: 1st order + follower
bullets: −26.6 dB at 50 Hz: 25 mV ≈ 0.05 LSB
Sufficient for the 3-bit ADC

right.head: Sallen-Key
bullets: −52 dB at 50 Hz: 1.4 mV ≈ 0.003 LSB
Margin for a higher-resolution ADC

slides.notes: 1 LSB = 0.5 V, so 25 mV is far below LSB/2. With 10 bits (LSB 3.9 mV) the first-order filter would leave about 6 LSB, the Sallen-Key less than half an LSB. Step response of the first-order filter: τ = 68 ms, 1 % after 0.31 s. Exercise 7.5.

slides.section: The Anti-Aliasing Filter of the Capstone
slides.title: Falstad: anti-aliasing filters

falstad.name: filter_antialias
falstad.hint: 2 V DC + 0.52 V at 50 Hz: compare the 50 Hz residue of both

observe: Both outputs settle to 2.00 V in about 0.3 s
Settling time stays short against the 200 ms sample period
slides.notes: Let the simulation run for about 0.6 s before reading the values. The input reproduces the capstone situation: 4.875 mV × 107.6 = 0.52 V of hum on the 2 V signal.

slides.section: The Anti-Aliasing Filter of the Capstone
slides.title: Twin-T notch at 50 Hz
bullets: Zero transmission at f_{0} = 1/(2πRC): 31.8 kΩ, 100 nF → 50 Hz
Removes 50 Hz almost completely (1 V → 0.45 mV)
Also attenuates 5 Hz (0.927), needs precise parts
Removes one frequency only: no replacement for the low-pass

falstad.name: filter_twin_t
falstad.hint: Compare Vout_5Hz and Vout_50Hz; detune one C and watch 50 Hz return

slides.notes: The twin-T needs a follower at its output. Exercise 7.6.

slides.section: The Anti-Aliasing Filter of the Capstone
slides.title: Design recipe: anti-aliasing low-pass
steps: Cutoff from the sample rate: f_{c} ≤ f_{s}/2 (capstone: 2.34 Hz at f_{s} = 5 Hz)
Attenuation: interference at the ADC must stay below LSB/2
1st order: choose C, R = 1/(2πf_{c}C), round so f_{c} ≤ f_{s}/2, buffer it
Check settling (≈ 5τ) and headroom: signal + hum must not clip
slides.notes: This is the design card at the end of the section. Capstone: 0.52 V × 0.047 = 25 mV, well below 250 mV.
